profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:46:52.672+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: The Grand Master for Protecting the State, Right Grand Master of Remonstrance, Acting Censor-in-Chief, Commissioner of Investigation and Rectification, Upholder of the State, bestowed with the Purple Gold Fish Pouch, your subject
by imperial decree compiles this work.
Later
Lù Démíng says: Qín
is the name of a valley in Lǒngxī,
northeast of Wūshǔ Shān in Yōngzhōu.
Fēizǐ, the ancestor of Qín,
pastured horses for King Xiào of Zhōu between the Qiān and Wèi Rivers.
He was enfeoffed as a dependent state,
and given the territory of Qín Gǔ.
Fēizǐ's great-grandson, Qín Zhòng,
was appointed Grand Master by King Xuān of Zhōu.
Zhòng's grandson, Xiānggōng,
defeated the Western Róng and saved Zhōu.
When King Píng moved his capital eastward,
he granted Xiānggōng the lands of Qí and Fēng,
elevating him to the rank of a feudal lord.
During the Spring and Autumn period, he was referred to as Bó of Qín.
King Zhāoxiāng
was named Jì,
a concubine's son of King Huìwén.
After the fall of Western Zhōu,
there was no one in the world suitable to be ruler.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance) dates events from King Zhāoxiāng's reign
because Qín eventually unified the world.
The rules for posthumous titles say: “Zhāo” signifies possessing virtue and having accomplished great deeds;
“Xiāng” signifies expanding territory and possessing virtue.
According to Shěn Yuè's rules for posthumous titles,
“Zhāoxiāng” is a double posthumous title.
卒 (zú),
pronounced zú.
諡 (shì),
pronounced shì.
辟 (bì),
read as pì.
Wáng Jī, the Governor of Hédōng, was executed in the marketplace
for colluding with other feudal lords.
Hédōng was originally Wèi territory.
Qín took it,
and because the land was east of the Great River,
established Hédōng Commandery.
守 (shǒu),
pronounced shǒu.
To execute a person in the marketplace
and abandon their body to the public.
Qín law decreed death in the marketplace
was called “abandonment in the marketplace.”
Wáng Jī recommended Fàn Suī to the King of Qín.
After Suī became chancellor of Qín,
Jī was also promoted.
Now, Jī died due to a crime,
so Suī became increasingly displeased.
懌 (yì),
means joy.
不懌 (bùyì),
means displeasure.
應 (yīng),
pronounced yīng.
Some say: When Fàn Suī was first employed by Qín
and then became chancellor,
King Zhāoxiāng was truly pleased with him.
After Zhèng Ānpíng surrendered to Zhào,
and Wáng Jī also fell into disfavor,
though Suī was chancellor,
King Zhāoxiāng, when presiding over court and meeting him,
became increasingly displeased.
懌 (yì),
pronounced yì.
The Marquis Yīng inquired about the reason.
The King said:
“Now Wǔ'ānjūn is dead,
and Zhèng Ānpíng, Wáng Jī, and others have all rebelled.
Internally we lack good generals, and externally we have many enemy states.
This is why I am worried!”
The Marquis Yīng was afraid,
not knowing what to do.
Cài Zé, a guest from Yān, heard of this
and traveled west to Qín.
He first sent someone to spread rumors to the Marquis Yīng, saying:
“Cài Zé
is the most eloquent man in the world.
When he sees the King,
he will surely cause you trouble and take your position.”
The Marquis Yīng was angered and
sent for him.
Cài Zé met the Marquis Yīng,
and his manners were arrogant.
The Marquis Yīng was displeased,
and thereupon reproached him, saying:
“You declared that you wish to replace me as chancellor.
Please let me hear your explanation.”
Cài Zé said:
“Xū!”
Kǒng Ānguó says: Xū
is an expression of doubt or surprise.
Kǒng Yǐngdá says: Xū is
a sound made when one has a suspicion in mind,
hence it is taken as an expression of doubt or surprise.
“Indeed, in the sequence of the four seasons,
those who have accomplished their task depart.”
This refers to spring giving birth,
summer growing,
autumn yielding fruit,
and winter storing away,
each accomplishing its task and replacing one another.
夫 (fú),
pronounced fú;
similarly below.
“What is there to desire?”
The deeds of Shāng Jūn are found in scroll 2, King Xiǎn of Zhōu, year 31.
The deeds of Wú Qǐ are found in scroll 1, King Ān, year 21.
Grand Master Zhǒng assisted King Gōujiàn of Yuè to wipe out the shame of Kuàijī.
He did not retire after his success and was killed by Gōujiàn.
种 (Zhǒng),
Wēn Gōng pronounces it zhāngyǒng fān.
与 (yǔ),
read as yú.
句 (gōu),
pronounced gōu.
踐 (jiàn),
pronounced jiàn.
种 (Zhǒng),
pronounced zhāngyǒng fān.
“Why not?
These three men
were the epitome of righteousness
and the ultimate in loyalty.
A noble person who sacrifices their life to achieve fame
has no regrets in death.”
Cài Zé said:
“Indeed, when a man achieves merit,
does he not hope for its complete fulfillment?
One whose person and fame are both complete
is superior;
one whose fame is worthy of emulation but whose person dies
is next;
one whose fame is disgraced and whose person remains whole
is inferior.
僇 (lù),
is the same as lù.
For a minister, exhausting loyalty and achieving merit
is indeed desirable.
Were not Hóng Yāo and Zhōu Gōng
also loyal and sagely?
How do the three men you mentioned compare
to Hóng Yāo and Zhōu Gōng in terms of desirability?”
Hóng Yāo
was a virtuous minister of King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu.
閎 (hóng),
pronounced hóng.
夭 (yāo),
pronounced yāo,
also yǎo.
“Good.”
Cài Zé said:
“In that case, does your lord treat old acquaintances generously
and not betray meritorious ministers
as well as Duke Xiào, the King of Chǔ, and the King of Yuè?”
He replied:
“I do not know how it compares.”
Cài Zé said:
“How do your achievements
compare to those three men?”
He replied:
“They are not as good.”
Cài Zé said:
“Then if you do not retire,
your troubles will likely be far greater than those of the three men.
The saying goes: ‘When the sun is at its zenith, it moves;
when the moon is full, it wanes.’
Advancing, retreating, expanding, and contracting—
for the five planets, appearing early is expanding,
appearing late is contracting.
嬴 (yíng),
pronounced yíng.
縮 (suō),
pronounced suō.
This is the way of the sages.
Now your grievances have been avenged and your kindness repaid—
grievances avenged refers to the killing of Wèi Qí;
kindness repaid refers to the promotion of Wáng Jī, Zhèng Ānpíng, and others.
I secretly fear for you!”
Thereupon, the Marquis Yīng
invited him to be his honored guest
and then recommended him to the King.
The King summoned him for a conversation,
was greatly pleased,
and appointed him guest minister.
The Marquis Yīng then pleaded illness and resigned.
The King, freshly pleased with Cài Zé's plans,
thereupon made him chancellor.
Zé was chancellor for several months
before being dismissed.
2 Chǔ Chūnshēn Jūn appointed Xún Qīng as Lánlíng lìng.
The Xìngpǔ (Genealogy of Surnames) says: Xún,
originally the surname Húán,
later the
"Yì" (radical for city/county)
was removed to form
"Xún."
Also, Jìn Xún Línfù
was a descendant of the ducal clan's Xí Shú.
The Bān Zhì (History of the Former Hàn Dynasty, Treatise on Geography) says:
Lánlíng Xiàn belonged to Dōnghǎi Jùn.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì (Correct Meaning of the Records of the Grand Historian) says: In modern Yízhōu Chéngxiàn there is Lánlíng Shān.
He was a man from Zhào,
named Kuàng.
He once debated military strategy with Línwǔ Jūn before Zhào Xiàochéng Wáng.
The King said:
"May I ask about the essentials of warfare?"
Línwǔ Jūn replied:
"To gain the opportune moment from heaven above,
to obtain geographical advantage below,
to observe the enemy's movements,
to strike after them,
but arrive before them—
this is the essential art of employing troops."
Hòu and Xiān
are both in the falling tone (qùshēng).
"No, that is not so.
What I have heard of the ancient way is that
the fundamental principle of all military campaigns and battles
lies in uniting the people.
If bows and arrows are not in harmony,
then Yì cannot hit the target with them;
if the six horses are not in accord,
then Zàofù cannot travel far with them;
Yì
was a skilled archer of ancient times;
Zàofù
was a skilled charioteer of ancient times.
Yì
is pronounced yì.
Zhòng
is pronounced as 'zhú zhòng' (falling tone).
Fù
is pronounced fǔ.
Then even Tāng and Wǔ could not be sure of victory.
Therefore, he who is good at attaching the people
is truly good at employing troops.
Thus, the essence of warfare lies merely in attaching the people."
Línwǔ Jūn said:
"No, that is not so.
What is valued in warfare is power and advantage,
and what is practiced is deception and trickery.
Those skilled in warfare are sudden and obscure;
Yáng Jìng says: Gǎnhū
means indistinct.
Yōu'àn
refers to the appearance of seeing vaguely from afar.
Sūn and Wú employed this
and were unrivaled in the world;
how could it be necessary to rely on attaching the people?"
Xún Qīng said:
"No, that is not so.
What I speak of
is the army of the benevolent,
the aspiration of a true king.
What you value
are schemes, power, and advantage.
The army of the benevolent
cannot be deceived.
Those who can be deceived
are the indolent,
the exposed and bare-bodied;
Lùtǎn
is like a person's limbs, upper and lower body, having no clothes to cover them,
being naked and bare-bodied.
Thus, to deceive a Jié with a Jié
is like a skillful and clumsy person having some luck.
To deceive a Yáo with a Jié
is comparable to throwing an egg at a rock,
or trying to bend boiling water with a finger.
It is like rushing into fire or water;
one enters and is burnt or drowned.
Therefore, the army of the benevolent,
from top to bottom, is of one mind,
the three armies united in strength.
The minister serves his ruler,
the subordinate serves his superior,
like a son serving his father,
or a younger brother serving his elder brother,
like arms protecting the head and eyes and covering the chest and abdomen.
To deceive and attack them
is the same as startling them first and then striking.
It is all one.
Moreover, when a benevolent ruler employs a state of ten li, he will have the listening of a hundred li;
when he employs a state of a hundred li, he will have the listening of a thousand li;
when he employs a state of a thousand li, he will have the listening of the four seas.
They will surely be intelligent and vigilant,
harmoniously united and consolidated.
Thus, the army of the benevolent,
when gathered, forms a troop;
a hundred men make a troop.
When extended, they are like the long blade of Mòyé;
Mòyé
was the treasured sword of Wú.
The Shuōwén says: Mòyé
is a long halberd.
Xié
is pronounced yé.
When pressed (or sharpened), they are like the sharp edge of Mòyé;
those who confront them are crushed.
"Duì"
in Liú Xiàng's Xīnxù is written as
"Ruì."
Yáng Jìng says: Duì
is like jù (gather),
read the same as duì (team).
Jìng
is pronounced liàng.
They are like a solid rock;
those who crash into it have their horns broken and retreat.
Furthermore, with whom will the ruler of a tyrannical state arrive?
With whom will the ruler of a tyrannical state arrive?
Those with whom he arrives
must be his people.
His people's affection for us is joyful like that for parents,
their fondness for us fragrant like pepper and orchids;
but when they turn to look at their own ruler, it is as if branded and tattooed,
as if looking at an enemy.
Human nature,
even for a Jié or Zhí,
how could anyone be willing to do what they dislike,
and harm what they love?
The Zìshū says: Chóu and Chóu
both mean 'a match.'
The Shuōwén says: Chóu (仇)
is Chóu (讎).
Chóu (讎)
is like 'to respond.'
The Zuǒzhuàn says: A hateful match is called chóu (仇).
The Jì says: One should not share the same sky
with the killer of one's father.
This probably refers to the initial matching of enemies.
When the match develops into resentment,
then it becomes chóu (仇).
Chóu (讎)
means 'to collate,'
two versions facing each other,
re-collating right and wrong.
When one suddenly faces the person who killed one's father,
and re-collates right and wrong,
then one will not share the same sky.
The meaning of chóu chóu (仇讎)
is most extreme here;
later generations generally adopted this usage.
Hào
is pronounced as 'hū dào' (falling tone).
Wéi
is pronounced as 'yú wěi' (falling tone).
È
is pronounced as 'wū lù' (falling tone).
They will surely come to inform us;
how then can he be deceived?
Therefore, when a benevolent person is employed,
the state grows brighter each day,
the feudal lords who submit first are secure,
those who submit later are endangered,
those who resist are diminished,
and those who revolt are destroyed.
The Shī (Book of Odes) says: 'Wǔ Wáng sets forth,
reverently grasping his axe,
like a blazing fire,
none dare oppose me.'
This is what is meant."
These are lines from the Shāng Sòng.
Wǔ Wáng
is Tāng.
Fā,
according to the Shāng Sòng, is read as pèi.
In ancient times, when a general was about to go to battle, he erected a flag.
King Xiào-Chéng and Lín-Wǔ-Jūn said:
“Excellent!
May I ask about the army of a true king,
what principles should be established,
and what actions taken to make it effective?”
Yáng Jìng said: “Shè (設)
means to establish and arrange.
Dào (道)
refers to discussions, teachings, and commands.
Xíng (行)
refers to mobilization and deployment.”
“Generally, when a ruler is virtuous, his state is well-governed;
when a ruler is incompetent, his state is in chaos.
Those who uphold ritual and value righteousness have well-governed states;
those who simplify ritual and despise righteousness have chaotic states.
A well-governed state is strong,
a chaotic state is weak;
this is the fundamental principle of strength and weakness.
If the superior is worthy of admiration, then the subordinates can be utilized;
if the superior is not worthy of admiration, then the subordinates cannot be utilized.
If subordinates can be utilized, the state is strong;
if subordinates cannot be utilized, the state is weak;
this is the constant principle of strength and weakness.
The people of Qí
highly valued 'jìjī'.
Mèng Kāng said: ‘Jìjī (技擊)
refers to the skills of military strategists,
training hands and feet,
proficient with weapons,
accumulating mechanisms,
to achieve victory in offense and defense.’
Yáng Jìng said: ‘Jì (技)
means talent and strength.
Qí people who used courage and strength to strike down enemies
were called 'jìjī'.
Lóng (隆)
means to value highly.
Jì (技)
is pronounced ‘qú qǐ fān’ (渠綺翻).
For acquiring one head, they were rewarded with a 'zī' of gold as redemption,
without any fundamental reward.”
Yáng Jìng said: “Eight liǎng (兩) is called a 'zī' (錙).
Běnshǎng (本賞),
refers to all those who have accomplishments receiving rewards equally.
Their 'jìjī' method was that if one obtained a head,
the government would reward them with 'zī' of gold to redeem it.
Beheading an enemy,
even if the battle was lost, still received a reward;
not beheading an enemy,
even if victorious, received no reward:
this meant there was no fundamental reward.”
Zī (錙)
is pronounced ‘zhuāng chí fān’ (莊持翻).
“Such an army can be used for minor skirmishes;
but when facing a formidable enemy,
it will scatter and disperse;
like birds in flight,
constantly shifting and turning without stability,
this is an army of a doomed state,
no army is weaker than this.
It is almost like hiring mercenaries to fight.
The Wǔzú of Wèi
were chosen by specific standards.
Yáng Jìng said: ‘They selected brave and valiant soldiers,
called Wǔzú (武卒).
Dù qǔ zhī (度取之)
means selecting those whose length, physique, and strength met the standards.’
Rú Chún said: ‘Sān (三)
refers to the body, yī (一)
to the thigh breeches, yī (一)
to the leg bindings,
totaling three components.’
Yī (衣)
is pronounced ‘yú jì fān’ (於既翻).
Shǔ (屬)
is pronounced ‘zhī yù fān’ (之欲翻).
Shěn Kuò said: ‘The 'shí' (石) of jūnjī shí (鈞石) is
one of the five measures;
one 'shí' weighs one hundred and twenty jīn (斤).
Later generations took one 'hú' (斛) to be one 'shí',
which was already the case since the Hàn dynasty,
as in the saying that Yú Dìng-Guó drank one 'shí' of wine without getting drunk.
Pulling strong bows and crossbows,
the ancients measured them by 'jūnjī shí'.
People today take the weight of one 'hú' of glutinous rice to be one 'shí';
generally, one 'shí' is ninety-two and a half jīn
according to the method, which is three hundred and forty-one jīn by Hàn scales.
Today's Wǔzú (武卒) can shoot a crossbow reaching nine 'shí' (石),
calculating their strength, it is equivalent to twenty-five 'shí' in ancient times,
compared to the Wǔzú of Wèi,
it would be more than two people.
There are bows that can be drawn three 'shí',
which is twenty-four 'jūn' (鈞) in ancient times,
compared to Yán Gāo's bow, it would be more than five people.
All this is due to recent training.
The flourishing of military preparations
has no parallel in ancient times.’
Upon examination, Kuò's discussion is detailed;
however, using these methods leads to national error and loss of an army,
not knowing how to adapt to changes,
this is Zhào Kuò's style of discussing warfare.”
Cāo (操)
is pronounced ‘qī dāo fān’ (七刀翻).
“Placing their 'gē' (戈) on top of their body,
meaning carrying the 'gē' (戈) on their body,
i.e., 'hé gē' (荷戈).
Hé (荷)
is pronounced ‘xià kě fān’ (下可翻).
Carrying three
days' provisions,
they would run a hundred 'lǐ' (里) by noon.
If they passed the test, their households would be exempt from corvée,
and their fields and residences would be made profitable.
Zhōng shì (中試),
means passing the measured test.
Fù qí hù (復其戶),
means exemption from corvée.
Lì qí tián zhái (利其田宅),
means being provided with convenient fields and residences.”
Zhòu (冑)
is today's 'dōumóu' (兜鍪).
Guān (冠)
is pronounced ‘gǔ wán fān’ (古玩翻).
Yíng (贏)
is pronounced ‘yí chéng fān’ (怡成翻),
meaning to carry.
Zhōng (中)
is pronounced ‘zhú zhòng fān’ (竹仲翻).
Fù (復)
is pronounced ‘fāng mù fān’ (方目翻).
“And the already granted exemptions and benefits cannot be taken away,
re-selecting would not be easy to do universally.
Gǎi zào (改造),
means to re-select.
Yì (易)
is pronounced ‘yì shì fān’ (弋豉翻).
Their taxes are certainly few;
this is an army that endangers the state.
The Qín people,
their lives are constrained and narrow,
their employment by the state is cruel and harsh.
They are coerced by power,
hidden in strategic passes,
made accustomed to rewards and praise,
and subjugated by punishments.”
Qiè (愜)
is the same as 'xiá' (狹).
Ài (隘)
is pronounced ‘wū xiè fān’ (烏懈翻).
Yáng Jìng said: “Yǐn zhī yǐ ài (隱之以阨),
means to conceal them in dangerous and strategic passes,
preventing enemies from harming them.”
Zhèng Shì said: “Qín territory has many strategic passes,
so its people are hidden within these passes.”
Niǔ (忸)
is the same as 'niǔ' (狃),
meaning to become accustomed to.
If they win battles, they are given rewards and praise,
making them accustomed to this as a regular practice.
Qiū (鰌)
means to oppress.
If they do not win, they are oppressed with punishments.
Zhuāngzǐ: ‘Wind said to the snake: qiū (鰌) me and also overcome me.’
Lù Dé-Míng's ‘Yīnyì’ (音義) says: ‘Qiū (鰌),
pronounced ‘qiū’,
means to oppress.’
Lǐ said: ‘Qiū (鰌),
means to oppress;
to oppress means to exploit.’”
Niǔ (忸)
is pronounced ‘nǚ jiǔ fān’ (女九翻).
“Without fighting, there is no way out.
They are made to continually seek rewards for merit.
Five armored heads entitle one to enslave five households.”
Yáng Jìng said: “Those with merit are rewarded,
making them continually seek more.
Anyone who obtains five armored heads can enslave five households in their locality.”
Yào (要)
is pronounced ‘yī yáo fān’ (一遙翻).
Zhǎng (長)
is pronounced ‘zhī liǎng fān’ (知兩翻).
“Thus, four generations achieved victory,
this was not by luck,
but by calculation.
Four generations
refer to Qín Xiào-Gōng, Huì-Wén-Wáng, Dào-Wǔ-Wáng,
and Zhāo-Xiāng-Wáng.
Wèi's Wǔzú could not contend with Qín's elite soldiers;
Qín's elite soldiers could not match the regulated discipline of Huán and Wén;
the regulated discipline of Huán and Wén could not withstand the benevolence and righteousness of Tāng and Wǔ.
Anyone who encounters them
is like throwing burnt crisp into a stone.
Burnt crisps are extremely brittle,
when thrown against a stone, they shatter.”
Áo (熬)
is pronounced ‘wǔ dāo fān’ (五刀翻).
“These are all soldiers who seek rewards and tread on profit,
a way of hiring and selling mercenaries;
there is no principle of honoring superiors, maintaining order, and upholding discipline.”
Yáng Jìng said: “Soldiers who seek rewards and tread on profit,
It is no different from hired laborers who sell their strength to work,
for whom there is no one who cherishes and values their superiors and is willing to die for them.
Content with the system,
they naturally do not overstep it.
Reaching the utmost in integrity and righteousness,
their minds do not conceive of wrongdoing.
Then they rise up and endanger them all.
Yáng Jìng says: "Subtlety" (微妙),
means to exhaust one's essence.
"Integrity" (節),
means benevolence and righteousness.
"Rise" (作),
means to stand up.
"Endanger" (殆),
means to imperil.
If a feudal lord can exhaust benevolence and righteousness,
then he will rise up and annex these several states,
bringing them to peril.
To exalt power and cunning,
and to value merit and profit,
is to gradually immerse them.
Jiàn (漸),
means to soak and steep.
It means that power, cunning, merit, and profit gradually permeate and become customs.
Jiàn (漸),
pronounced zī lián (子廉) fān (翻).
This is to bring them into uniformity.
Therefore, to meet cunning with cunning,
there is still skill and clumsiness;
to meet cunning with uniformity,
it is like dropping a pointed awl or a knife onto Tài Shān (泰山).
It means that against those brought into uniformity by ritual, righteousness, teaching, and transformation,
to meet them with cunning,
none will fail to be defeated.
Duò (墮),
should be read as huī (隳).
With clasped hands and a wave of the command,
the strong and violent states all rush to serve,
executing Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂) as if executing a lone tyrant.
Therefore, the "Tài Shì" (泰誓) says: 'The lone tyrant Zhòu (紂),'
this is what it means.
Therefore, a great uniformity in military affairs controls the world;
a small uniformity governs neighboring enemies.
As for troops that are recruited and selected,
that exalt power and cunning,
and value merit and profit,
their victories and defeats are not constant;
they alternately contract and expand,
alternately exist and perish,
vying for supremacy against each other.
This is called a "robber army,"
which a jūn zǐ (君子) does not follow."
Xiào Chéng Wáng (孝成王) and Lín Wǔ Jūn (臨武君) said:
"Excellent.
May we ask about being a general?"
Xún Qīng (荀卿) said:

3 Initially,
during the time of Qí Wēi and Xuān,
Zōu Yǎn authored treatises on the cycle of the Five Virtues from beginning to end.
The so-called cycle of the Five Virtues from beginning to end is as follows: Fúxī ruled by Wood virtue;
Wood engenders Fire,
hence Shénnóng ruled by Fire virtue;
Fire engenders Earth,
hence Huángdì ruled by Earth virtue;
Earth engenders Metal,
hence Shàohào ruled by Metal virtue;
Metal engenders Water,
hence Zhuānxū ruled by Water virtue;
Water engenders Wood,
hence Dìkù again ruled by Wood virtue;
Wood again engenders Fire,
hence Dì Yáo ruled by Fire virtue;
Fire again engenders Earth,
hence Dì Shùn ruled by Earth virtue;
Earth again engenders Metal,
hence Xià ruled by Metal virtue;
Metal again engenders Water,
hence Shāng ruled by Water virtue;
Water again engenders Wood,
hence Zhōu ruled by Wood virtue:
this is the cycle of the Five Virtues ending and restarting.
Zōu Yǎn believed that Zhōu acquired Fire virtue,
probably because the flow of fire in Wángwū was seen as an auspicious sign for Zhōu's reception of the mandate,
and also because their clothing and colors favored red.
Following Yǎn's theory of the beginning and end,
Qín should have adopted Earth as its virtue.
However, Shǐhuáng now takes Water to overcome Fire,
considering Water as his virtue,
which is known as "promoting the overcoming element" (tuī wǔ shèng 推五勝).
Early Hàn took Earth as its virtue,
which also probably followed Yǎn's theory.
The people of Qí presented this [theory].
Shǐhuáng adopted his theory,
believing that Zhōu possessed Fire virtue,
and Qín replaced Zhōu,
taking the element that overcomes Fire,
which is Water virtue.

The sentence "改年" (changed the year) is punctuated.
The Xià dynasty took the month in which the Big Dipper's handle pointed to Yín (寅) as the beginning of the year;
the Yīn dynasty took the month in which the Big Dipper's handle pointed to Chǒu (丑) as the beginning of the year;
the Zhōu dynasty took the month in which the Big Dipper's handle pointed to Zǐ (子) as the beginning of the year.
Now Shǐhuáng took the month in which the Big Dipper's handle pointed to Hài (亥) as the beginning of the year,
which is a change of the year.
From this point, all calendar years began in the tenth month,
with court greetings on the first day of the tenth month.
As Water was taken as the virtue,
the color black was favored,
and since the number associated with Water is six,
six was used as the basis for calculations.

【Zhāng: The twelve-line edition lacks these eight characters;
the eleven-line edition of Yǐ is the same.
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day wù yín,
a great amnesty was granted.
2 In spring,
Èr Shì traveled eastward through the commanderies and counties.
Lǐ Sī followed him.
They reached Jié Shí,
proceeded along the coast,
and southward to Kuài Jī.
There, he fully inscribed the stone tablets that Shǐ Huáng had inscribed,
with the names of the accompanying great ministers
to glorify the former emperor's achievements and great virtues, and then returned.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Èr Shì arrived at Xián Yáng.
He said to Zhào Gāo:
"Indeed, human life in the world
is like a six-horse chariot speeding past a crack in the wall.
Now that I have taken control of the world,
I wish to fully enjoy all that my ears and eyes desire,
and exhaust all the pleasures of my heart and mind,
to complete my allotted years.
Is this permissible?"
Gāo replied:
"This is what a worthy ruler can do, but what a foolish and chaotic ruler is forbidden to do.
Nevertheless,
though such enjoyment is not yet permissible,
your subject requests to speak about it: The plot at Shā Qiū
was doubted by all the imperial princes and great ministers.
And all the imperial princes are the emperor's elder brothers;
the great ministers were also appointed by the former emperor.
Now that Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
these individuals are likely discontent and unsubmissive,
fearing a change.
Your subject is constantly trembling with fear,
only fearing that it will not last.
How can Your Majesty indulge in such pleasures?"
Èr Shì asked:
"What should be done about it?"
Zhào Gāo replied:
"Your Majesty should strictly enforce laws and impose harsh punishments,
making those with guilt implicate each other,
and execute great ministers and members of the imperial clan.
Then, collect the remaining populace,
enrich the poor,
and elevate the humble.
Completely remove the former emperor's old ministers,
and replace them with those whom Your Majesty personally trusts.
This way, hidden virtues will belong to Your Majesty,
harm will be eliminated, and treacherous plots will be suppressed.
None of your subjects will fail to receive your bounty
and partake in your great favor.
Your Majesty will then be able to rest easy and indulge freely in pleasures.
There is no better plan than this!"
Èr Shì agreed.
Thereupon, he revised the laws,
striving to make them even harsher and more severe.
If great ministers or imperial princes were found guilty,
they were immediately sent to Gāo
for interrogation and judgment.
Consequently, twelve imperial princes were executed in the market of Xián Yáng,
and ten princesses were crushed to death in Dù.
Their wealth was confiscated by the county officials.
The Hàn referred to the Son of Heaven as "county official" (xiàn guān).
Here, "xiàn guān"
means "the public treasury."
It is said that when affairs were interconnected, all implicated individuals were arrested.
Gòng Fù said: If the person is present,
to directly pursue and seize them is "dǎi";
if the person is absent,
then to pursue and capture them.
"Dǎi" (逮)
is an easy word;
"bǔ" (捕)
implies exerting force.
Gōngzǐ Jiānglǘ (公子將閭) and his two brothers were imprisoned in the inner palace.
Their crimes were discussed, and his was considered last.
Èrshì (二世) sent an envoy to Gōngzǐ Jiānglǘ, saying:
"You, Gōngzǐ (公子), have been disloyal as a subject.
Your crime warrants death!"
The officer carried out the judgment.
Jiānglǘ (將閭) said:
"Regarding the rites in the palace court,
I never dared not follow the ritual master's guidance;
regarding my position in the ancestral temple,
I never dared to lose my integrity;
when receiving commands and responding,
I never dared to err in my words;
how can I be called disloyal as a subject?
I dared not rely on the affection of kinship to abandon my duties as a subject.
How can this crime be imposed upon me?
The envoy said:
"I am not permitted to deliberate on this matter.
I merely carry out the orders written in the dispatch!"
Jiānglǘ (將閭) then looked up to heaven and cried out
"Heaven!"
three times,
saying:
"I am innocent!"
All three brothers wept,
drew their swords, and committed suicide.
The imperial clan was greatly terrified.
Gōngzǐ Gāo (公子高) wanted to flee,
but feared his clan would be exterminated,
so he submitted a memorial which read:
"When the late emperor was alive,
when I entered the palace
I was granted food,
and when I went out I was allowed to ride in his carriage.
I was granted clothes from the imperial wardrobe,
and I received them.
I was granted the precious horses from the imperial stables,
and I received them.
I ought to have died with him but failed to do so,
thus I am unfilial as a son,
and disloyal as a subject.
One who is unfilial and disloyal
has no reputation to stand upon in the world.
I request to follow him in death,
and I wish to be buried at the foot of Lìshān (驪山).
I only hope Your Majesty will mercifully grant this!"
When the memorial was submitted,
Èrshì (二世) was greatly pleased,
summoned Zhào Gāo (趙高) and showed it to him,
saying:
"Can this be called urgent?"
Zhào Gāo (趙高) said:
"A subject should be too preoccupied with the fear of death to have time for other schemes!"
Èrshì (二世) approved his memorial,
and granted him one hundred thousand cash for his burial.
The Āfánggōng (阿房宮) was rebuilt.
All of the fifty thousand able-bodied men were conscripted to form a garrison guard in Xiányáng (咸陽),
and ordered to practice archery.
As there were many dogs, horses, birds, and beasts to be fed,
and the supply was deemed insufficient,
an order was issued to the commanderies and counties
to transport beans, millet, straw, and hay.
All were ordered to bring their own provisions.
Within three hundred *lǐ* (里) of Xiányáng (咸陽),
it was forbidden to eat locally grown grain.
3 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Chén Shèng from Yángchéng and Wú Guǎng from Yángxià raised an army in Qí.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: This refers to Yángchéng County in Hénán;
The Bān Zhì [i.e., Hàn Shū Dìlǐ Zhì]
placed it under Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Yángxià County belonged to Huáiyáng Kingdom.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Táikāng County in Chénzhōu
was originally the land of Hàn Yángxià County.
Pánzhōu Hóng Shì said: Yángxià Township is thirty lǐ away from Táikāng County.
Xià,
is pronounced jiǎ.
The Bān Zhì states:
Qí County belonged to Pèi Commandery,
and contained Dàzé Township.
Qí,
is pronounced qúyī.
They were conscripted from the lǘzuǒ to garrison Yúyáng.
Cháo Cuò said: Qín sent convicts to garrison,
first sending officials with infractions, as well as z赘xù (men who married into their wives' families) and merchants,
then those who had previously been registered as merchants,
and then those whose grandparents had previously been registered as merchants,
and finally took from the lǘ, those on the left.
The Suǒyǐn states: Lǘzuǒ
refers to those living on the left of the lǘlǐ.
During the Qín dynasty,
those who had tax exemptions resided on the left of the lǘ.
Now, all those in the lǘzuǒ who were capable of labor were conscripted.
It also says: Generally, the wealthy and powerful were on the right,
and the poor and weak were on the left.
Many of those conscripted by Qín for garrison duty were wealthy;
when these were exhausted,
they also took from the poor and weak to conscript them.
The Bān Zhì states:
Yúyáng County belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Yúyáng was eighteen lǐ south of Mìyún County in Tánzhōu,
on the sunny side of the Yú River.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng were both túnbá (company commanders).
Shīgǔ said: A tún is where people gather.
Zhǎng
means commander.
There was a great rain,
blocking the roads,
and they realized they had already missed the deadline;
missing the deadline
was punishable by decapitation according to the law.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng, taking advantage of the widespread discontent,
then killed the jiāngwèi (commander and adjutant).
Shīgǔ said: Their official title was originally wèì,
but at that time, they commanded garrison troops,
hence they were called jiāngwèi.
The Suǒyǐn states: Wèi
is an official title;
according to the Hàn Jiùyí, there were three in a large county.
Their wèì commanded a tún of nine hundred men,
hence they were called jiāngwèi.
"You all have missed the deadline and are to be executed;
even if we are not executed,
six or seven out of ten of those garrisoned will die anyway.
Moreover, a true warrior, if not to die, then so be it;
but if to die, then let it be for a great name!
Are kings, marquises, generals, and chancellors born with their status?"
All the men agreed.
They then falsely claimed to be Gōngzǐ Fúsū and Xiàng Yàn,
because the common people respected Fúsū and the Chu people pitied Xiàng Yàn.
They proclaimed "Great Chǔ";
Chén Shèng established himself as a jiāngjūn (general),
and Wú Guǎng as a dūwèi (commandant).
They attacked Dàzé Township,
and took it;
they gathered its forces and attacked Qí,
and Qí surrendered.
They gathered the soldiers from Dàzé Township to attack Qí.
They attacked Zhì, Cuó, Kǔ, Zhè, and Qiáo,
and all of them surrendered.
The Bān Zhì states: Fúlǐ, Zhì, Cuó, and Qiáo belonged to Pèi Commandery.
The Xìngpǔ states: After the Gě state was destroyed,
its descendants took the state's name as their surname.
Zhè
and Kǔ counties belonged to Huáiyáng Kingdom.
Sòng Bái said: Zhè County
was the ancient city of Xiāngshì;
during the Spring and Autumn period, it was Zhūyě of Chén;
during the Hàn dynasty, it was Zhè County,
named after the Zhègōu canal in the city;
during the Táng dynasty, it was Zhèchéng County in Sòngzhōu.
Zhēnyuán County in Bózhōu
was the land of ancient Kǔ County.
Xún,
pronounced cíjùnfān,
means to conquer territory.
Zhì,
pronounced zhúyǐfān.
"Cuó,"
originally written as
pronounced cáiduōfān.
Shīgǔ said: This county originally borrowed the character "酇" for its name,
pronounced cuó.
Wáng Mǎng changed the county name to Zànzhì,
so this county also had the zàn sound.
Kǔ,
pronounced hù.
By the time they reached Chén,
they had six or seven hundred chariots,
over a thousand cavalry,
and tens of thousands of infantry.
They attacked Chén.
The Chén shǒu (administrator) and wèi (adjutant) were both absent.
Only the shǒuchéng (acting assistant administrator) fought them within the qiáomén (gate tower),
but he was defeated;
the shǒuchéng died,
and Chén Shèng then entered and occupied Chén.
The Bān Zhì states:
Chén County belonged to Huáiyáng Kingdom.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: The present-day Chénzhōu city was originally the city of the Chén kingdom built by King Xiāng of Chǔ.
Shīgǔ said: Shǒuchéng
refers to the commandery assistant administrator who was guarding;
another explanation is: the assistant administrator of the commandery administrator,
hence called shǒuchéng.
Yuánfù said: Qín did not establish Chén as a commandery,
so why would it have a shǒu?
Shǒu
here refers to a non-regular official,
merely an acting one.
I note that Qín divided the realm into commanderies and counties.
A commandery had a shǒu, wèi, and jiān,
and a county had a lìng, céng, and wèi.
Yuánfù's view that this shǒu was an acting one
is correct.
Qiān [i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān's Shǐjì] and Gù [i.e., Bān Gù's Hàn Shū] both write
"the shǒulìng (administrator and magistrate) were both absent,"
while this text writes
"the shǒuwèi (administrator and adjutant) were both absent."
Perhaps in the two histories,
after lìng,
the character wèi
is missing,
and in the Tōngjiàn,
before wèi,
the character lìng
is missing.
Shīgǔ said: Qiáomén
refers to a high tower built above the gate for observation.
A tower
is also called qiáo,
hence a beautiful tower is called a lìqiáo;
it is also called a cháo.
What is called a cháochē
is also a tower built on top of a war chariot to observe the enemy.
Qiáo and cháo
are similar in sound.
Initially,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú, natives of Dàliáng, had become sworn brothers, pledging loyalty unto death.
When Qín extinguished Wèi,
it heard that the two were famous scholars of Wèi,
and offered a heavy reward for their capture.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú then changed their names,
and both went to Chén.
They worked as village gatekeepers to support themselves.
Shī Gǔ said: "Gatekeepers
were the lowliest of soldiers;
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú concealed themselves among the humble and lowly."
Zhāng Yàn said: "Gatekeepers
were the guards of the village head."
監 (jiān),
is pronounced like 'xián' in ancient times.
Chén Yú wanted to rise,
but Zhāng Ěr stepped on his foot,
making him endure a beating.
"Wanted to rise"
means he could not bear the humiliation
and wanted to fight back against the official.
躡 (niè),
is pronounced 'niè' (nié)
and means to step on one's foot.
笞 (chī),
is pronounced 'chī'.
Zhāng Ěr then led Chén Yú to the shade of a mulberry tree
and admonished him, saying:
"What did I discuss with you in the beginning?
Now you suffer a slight insult and wish to die for one official!"
Chén Yú apologized.
When Chén Shè had entered Chén,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú went to his gate to request an audience.
Chén Shèng's
courtesy name was Shè.
He was greatly pleased.
The local heroes, magnates, and elders of Chén requested that Shè be enthroned as King of Chǔ.
Shè consulted Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú about this.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú replied:
"Qín has been lawless,
destroying people's states,
and tyrannizing the populace.
Your general launched a plan risking ten thousand deaths,
to eliminate the oppressors for the world.
Now, as soon as you arrive in Chén, if you crown yourself king,
you will show the world your selfishness.
We wish that Your General would not become king,
but quickly lead your troops west;
send people to enthrone the descendants of the Six States,
thereby forming your own factions
and increasing Qín's enemies.
With more enemies, their strength will be divided;
with more allies, your army will be strong.
If this is done,
then there will be no clashes of arms in the field;
the Six States will all become allied states,
and no armies will engage in combat in the wilderness.
All counties will revolt against Qín and return to being great states,
with no one left to defend cities for Qín.
Occupy Xiányáng,
and command the feudal lords;
the feudal lords, having been overthrown and then re-established,
will be subdued by your virtue,
and thus
the imperial enterprise will be accomplished!
If you alone become king in Chén now,
we fear the world will slacken."
Chén Shè did not listen,
and thereupon enthroned himself as king,
styling himself
"Zhāng Chǔ."
Liú Dé said: "This means 'to expand the state of Chǔ'."
Zhāng Yàn said: "Before this, Chǔ had already been extinguished by Qín;
now, Chǔ is re-established as Zhāng."
At that time,
the various commanderies and counties suffered under Qín's laws
and competed to kill their chief officials in response to Shè.
An usher
came from the east
and reported the rebels.
Èr Shì was enraged
and handed him over to the officials.
Later, another envoy arrived;
the emperor questioned him,
and he replied:
"They are mere bandits, sneaking around like rats and dogs.
The commandery governors and commandants are currently pursuing and capturing them.
They have all been caught now,
and there is nothing to worry about."
The emperor was pleased.
King Chén appointed Wú Shū as acting king,
to oversee the generals in attacking Xíngyáng to the west.
Wú Guǎng's
courtesy name was Shū.
Xíngyáng County belonged to Sānchuān Commandery.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú again advised King Chén,
requesting an elite force to march north and conquer the territory of Zhào.
Thereupon, King Chén appointed Wǔ Chén, a native of Chén whom he had previously befriended, as general,
and Shào Sāo as Protector of the Army.
The Xìng Pǔ says: "The Wǔ surname
is descended from Sòng Wǔgōng."
I (the commentator) say: "Since there is an established method for posthumous titles,
many have been given 'Wǔ' as a posthumous title,
so why must the Wǔ surname necessarily be descended from Sòng Wǔgōng?
What a rigid interpretation!"
The Táng Records of Clans consider the Wǔ clan to be descended from the Jī surname,
stating that a younger son of King Píng of Zhōu was born with the character
'Wǔ'
written on his hand, and thus adopted it as his surname.
This is a fabricated account influenced by Empress Wǔ.
Zhào Míngchéng's Jīnshí Lù contains the stele of Wǔ Bān, Prefect of Dūnhuáng in the Hàn dynasty, which states: "In ancient times, King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn conquered Guǐfāng,
and his official clan divided, taking this as their surname."
The Shào surname
is descended from Shào Gōng Shì, a son of King Wén of Zhōu;
some say it is descended from Dān Jìzài, his eleventh son.
He was given three thousand men
to conquer Zhào.
King Chén also ordered Dèng Zōng, a man from Rǔyīn, to conquer Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn enfeoffed his uncle north of the Hé River,
who became Dèng Hóu,
and later adopted this as his surname.
The Bān Records state that Rǔyīn County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery,
formerly the state of Hú.
Jiǔjiāng,
originally Chǔ territory,
was divided by Qín after it destroyed Chǔ to establish Jiǔjiāng Commandery;
Xiàng Yǔ destroyed Qín and enfeoffed Qíng Bù there;
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn renamed it Huáinán State;
Emperor Wǔ later called it Jiǔjiāng Commandery again.
There were countless groups of several thousand Chǔ soldiers gathering.
Gě Yīng reached Dōngchéng.
The Bān Records state that Dōngchéng County
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
The Kuò Dì Zhì says: "The old city of Dōngchéng
is fifty lí southeast of Dìngyuǎn County, Háozhōu."
The Xìng Pǔ: "Xiāng
is descended from Xiāng Qiáng, a son of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ."
He then killed Xiāng Qiáng and returned to report.
King Chén executed Gě Yīng.
King Chén ordered
Zhōu Shì to march north and conquer Wèi territory.
He appointed Cài Cì, Lord of Fáng, a man from Shàngcài, as Supreme Commander.
Suǒyǐn says: "Fáng
is a place name;
ennobling someone to Fáng,
he was called Lord of Fáng."
Supreme Commander (shàng zhù guó)
was the most esteemed rank in Chǔ.
Cài
adopted the state name as their surname.
King Chén heard that Zhōu Wén,
a worthy man from Chén,
was skilled in military matters.
So he gave him the general's seal
and sent him to attack Qín to the west.
Wǔ Shén and others crossed the river from Báimǎ.
Shīgǔ said: Báimǎjīn (Báimǎ Ford) is now within the boundaries of Báimǎ County, Huázhōu.
Guādìzhì says: Báimǎ Gùchéng (Old City of Báimǎ),
is twenty-four *lǐ* southwest of Wèinán County, Huázhōu.
Dài Yánzhī’s Xīzhēngjì (Record of the Western Expedition) says: Báimǎ Gùchéng is the Cao邑 (Cao Settlement) of Wèi.
He spoke to the local heroes,
and the heroes all responded;
so he went to gather troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men;
they acclaimed Wǔ Shén as Wǔxìn Jūn.
They captured more than ten cities in Zhào,
while the rest remained fortified;
so he led his troops northeast to attack Fányáng.
Bānzhì says,
Fányáng County belonged to Zhuó Jùn.
Yìng Shào said: It is on the sunny side of the Fán River.
Kuǎi Chè,
is Kuǎi Tōng.
Bānshū (Book of Han) avoided the taboo name of Emperor Wǔ,
changing
“Chè”
to
“Tōng”.
Kuǎi,
pronounced *qiū guài*,
is a surname.
Zuǒzhuàn says,
the state of Jìn had a grandee named Kuǎi Dé.
“Your Excellency must first win battles before taking territory,
and only after capturing them can you take cities.
I secretly believe this to be a mistake.
If you sincerely follow my plan,
cities can be surrendered without attack,
territory taken without battle,
and a thousand *lǐ* can be pacified by simply sending a dispatch;
is this possible?”
Shīgǔ said: A *xí* (dispatch)
is a letter written on a bamboo slip,
one foot two inches long,
used for summons;
if urgent,
bird feathers were added and inserted,
to indicate extreme urgency.
Xí,
pronounced *hù lì*.
“What do you mean?”
Chè said:
“The Magistrate of Fányáng, Xú Gōng,
fears death and is greedy,
wishing to surrender first.
If you treat him as an official appointed by Qín,
executing him as you did the previous ten cities,
then all border cities will become like ‘metal walls and boiling moats,’
unassailable.
If you bestow upon your servant a marquis’s seal to give to the Magistrate of Fányáng,
enabling him to ride in a Vermilion-wheeled, Flowery-spoked carriage,
galloping through the suburbs of Yān and Zhào,
then the cities of Yān and Zhào can be surrendered without battle.”
Wǔxìn Jūn said:
“Excellent!”
He sent a hundred chariots, two hundred cavalry, and a marquis’s seal to welcome Xú Gōng.
When Yān and Zhào heard of this,
over thirty cities surrendered without fighting.
After Chén Wáng dispatched Zhōu Zhāng,
he, due to the chaos of Qín’s government,
developed a slighting attitude towards Qín,
and no longer maintained his defenses.
The Erudite Kǒng Fù admonished him, saying:
Fù,
was the son of Wèi Xiàng Zǐ Shùn,
and an eighth-generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ (Confucius),
the one who earlier concealed the books.
“Your servant has heard a military maxim: ‘Do not rely on the enemy not attacking me,
but rely on my being unassailable.’
Now the King relies on the enemy and not on himself;
if he stumbles and cannot recover,
repentance will be too late.”
Chén Wáng said:
“Do not burden yourself with my army, Sir.”
Zhōu Wén gathered troops as he advanced to the Pass,
with a thousand chariots and several hundred thousand soldiers.
They reached Xì,
and encamped there.
Shīgǔ said: Xì
is a river name,
east of Xīnfēng, Jīngzhào;
today there is a Xìshuǐ post station.
Its water originally flowed from the northern boundary of Lántián,
and at this point flowed north into the Wèi River.
Sū Lín said: Xì is thirty *lǐ* southeast of Xīnfēng.
Xì,
pronounced *xǔ xuān*.
Yīn Shìchén deliberated, saying:
“What should we do?”
The Grand Steward Zhāng Hán said:
Bānbiǎo says: The Grand Steward,
a Qín official,
was in charge of taxes from mountains, forests, ponds, and marshes to supply the imperial household.
Xìngpǔ says: People from Qí surrendered to Zhāng,
their descendants removed the *yì* (city/settlement) radical to become the Zhāng clan.
Shǎo,
pronounced *shī zhào*.
Hán,
pronounced *xià gān*.
“The bandits have arrived,
their forces are strong;
to dispatch troops from nearby counties now
is too late.
There are many laborers at Líshān;
Qín convicts who have already been judged
are sent to labor at Líshān.
Arm them to strike the enemy.”
Èr Shì thereupon granted a great amnesty to all under Heaven,
and had Zhāng Hán exempt the Líshān laborers and the children born to household slaves,
raising them all to attack the Chǔ army,
and utterly defeated them.
Fú Qián said: *Rénnú chǎnzǐ* refers to children born to household slaves.
Shīgǔ said: *Núcǎnzǐ* is like what people today call *jiāshēngnú* (household-born slaves).
Zhòng Fēng said: *Rénnú* is one type of thing, *chǎnzǐ* is another type.
Chén Zàn said: *Rénnú zhī chǎnzǐ* are like today’s tenant farmers’ children.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú arrived at Hándān,
heard that Zhōu Zhāng had been repelled,
and also heard that many generals who had campaigned for Chén Wáng had been slandered, found guilty, and executed upon their return.
So they persuaded Wǔxìn Jūn to declare himself king.
In the eighth month,
Wǔxìn Jūn declared himself King of Zhào,
appointed Chén Yú as Grand General,
Bānbiǎo: Front, Rear, Left, and Right Generals,
were offices of the late Zhōu dynasty,
Qín adopted them,
holding the rank of Upper Minister.
In Hàn, the Grand General was among the three Ducal Ministers.
and Shào Sāo as Left Chancellor;
he sent someone to report to Chén Wáng.
Chén Wáng was greatly enraged,
wishing to exterminate the families of Wǔxìn Jūn and others and dispatch troops to attack Zhào.
The Pillar of State, Fáng Jūn, admonished him, saying:
“Qín has not yet perished, and if you execute the families of Wǔxìn Jūn and others,
this would be creating another Qín;
it is better to seize the opportunity to congratulate them,
and have them urgently lead troops west to attack Qín.”
Chén Wáng thought this was correct,
and followed his plan,

Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú persuaded the King of Zhào, saying:

Yān,
is the land north of Zhuó Jùn.
Dài,
is the land north of Chángshān.
Hénèi was originally Wèi territory,
at that time belonging to Hédōng Jùn.
With Yān and Dài to the north,
even if Chǔ defeats Qín,
they will certainly not dare to control Zhào;
if they do not defeat Qín,
they will surely value Zhào.
Zhào, taking advantage of the exhaustion of Qín and Chǔ,
can achieve its ambitions over all under Heaven.”
The King of Zhào considered this correct,
and consequently did not send troops west,
but instead sent Hán Guǎng to campaign in Yān,
Lǐ Liáng to campaign in Chángshān,
and Zhāng Yǎn to campaign in Shàngdǎng.
In the ninth month,
Liú Bāng of Pèi raised an army in Pèi.
When the Táo Táng shì clan had declined,
a descendant of theirs, Liú Lěi,

Pèi,

Initially, he was the Tíngzhǎng of Sìshàng.
Qín law: one *tíng* every ten *lǐ*.

A physiognomist

Shàn,

Máng,
pronounced Máng.
Dàng,
pronounced Táng;

When the young men of Pèi heard of this,
many wished to join him.
When Chén Shè rose up,
the Pèi Magistrate wanted to respond to him with Pèi.
Clerk Xiāo Hé and Chief Administrator Cáo Cān said:
According to the biography of Cáo Cān,
Cān was a clerk, and Hé was the Chief Administrator.

was the *gōngcáo*.

Shù,

Yuàn,
pronounced Yú Juàn.
"You are an official of Qín;

So he ordered Fán Kuài to summon Liú Jì.
Liú Jì's followers already numbered several hundred;

intending to execute Xiāo and Cáo.
Xiāo and Cáo were afraid,
so they scaled the city wall and sought refuge with Liú Jì.
This means they pledged allegiance to Liú Jì to ensure their safety.
They sent a message to the elders of Pèi,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
The elders then led their young men to collectively kill the Pèi Magistrate,
opened the gates to welcome Liú Jì,
and installed him as Pèi Gōng.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Chǔ usurped the title of King,
and many of its high officials were enfeoffed as *xiàn gōng* (county lords),
such as Shēn Gōng, Yè Gōng, and Lǔyáng Gōng.
Now, installing Jì as Pèi Gōng
was using the Chǔ system.
He gained three
thousand men
to respond to the other lords.
Xiàng Liáng was
the son of the Chu general Xiàng Yàn.
He once killed a man,
and with his nephew Jì, avoided revenge in Wúzhōng.
All the worthy gentry and officials of Wúzhōng were subordinate to him.
When Jì was young, he studied calligraphy,
but failed to master it
and quit.
He studied swordsmanship,
but also failed.
Xiàng Liáng was angry with him.
Jì said,
"Calligraphy
is only good enough for writing one's name!
Swordsmanship,
to fight one person is not worth learning;

Thereupon, Xiàng Liáng taught Jì military strategy,
and Jì was greatly pleased.
He grasped the general idea,
but again refused to complete his studies.
Jì was over eight *chǐ* tall,
and strong enough to lift a *dǐng*.

means to lift.
Suǒyǐn said: *Shuōwén* states: *gáng*

*Zhǎng*,
read *zhēn liàng fān*.
*Gáng*,

Yīn Tōng, the Administrator of Kuàijī,
Xú Guǎng said: At that time, it was not yet called *tàishǒu*.

*Xìngpǔ* says: When King Wǔ conquered Shāng,

*Shǒu*,
read *shì yòu fān*;
same below.
wanted to raise troops to respond to Shè.
He sent Xiàng Liáng and Huán Chǔ as generals.
At this time,
Huán Chǔ was a fugitive hiding in the marshes.
Liáng said,

Liáng then
instructed Jì to stand outside with his sword.
Liáng re-entered

The Administrator said,

Liáng summoned Jì in.

Xiàng Liáng held the Administrator's head

*Shìmíng* says: *Yìn*,
means "trust,"

*Shòu*,

three *chǐ* wide,

There was chaos.
Jì struck and killed dozens to a hundred people.
It means the number of people he killed ranged from dozens to a hundred.
No one dared to rise up.
Liáng then summoned the local influential officials he knew,

He sent men to gather the lower counties.
Lower counties

Liáng became the Administrator of Kuàijī,
and Jì became a second general,

Jì was twenty-four years old at this time.
Such was Xiàng Jì.
Tián Dān was
a member of the former royal family of Qí.
Dān's younger cousin Róng,
and Róng's younger brother Héng,
were all powerful and strong,
with a strong clan,
and capable of attracting people.
Zhōu Shì campaigned to Dì,
Zhōu Shì was from Wèi.
Tián Dān pretended to bind his slave,
went to the court with some youths,
intending to request permission to kill the slave.
When he saw the Magistrate of Dì,
he consequently struck and killed the Magistrate.
Then he summoned the sons of powerful officials, saying,
"All the lords have rebelled against Qín and established themselves.
Qí
was an ancient established state;
Dān,
of the Tián clan,

Thereupon, he established himself as King of Qí,

Zhōu Shì's army returned and left.
Tián Dān led his troops east to conquer and pacify the Qí territory.
Hán Guǎng led troops north to campaign in Yān.
The powerful figures of Yān wanted to jointly establish Guǎng as King of Yān.
Guǎng said,
"My mother is in Zhào,

The Yān people said,
"Zhào is now worried about Qín in the west

Moreover, with Chǔ's strength,

How would Zhào alone dare to harm your general's family?"
Hán Guǎng then established himself as King of Yān.
Several months later,
the family members of the King of Zhào and Yān's mother returned to him.
The King of Zhào, along with Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú, went north to campaign in the Yān border region.
The King of Zhào secretly slipped out.
Shī Gǔ said: This means to secretly leave by taking advantage of a gap.
Yān imprisoned him,
wanting to demand cession of territory.
Envoys went to request his release,

A servant soldier ran to the Yān camp.
Rú Chún said: *sī*

*Sī*,
sound *sī*.
*Yǎng*,
read *yáng shàng fān*.
"Do you know what Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú want?"

The Zhào servant soldier laughed and said,

Those Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú,

How could they wish to remain generals and ministers forever?!
It's just that their power was newly established,
and they dared not yet divide and rule as three kings,
*cān*
is like *sān* (three).
so as to maintain Zhào's allegiance.
Now that Zhào's territory is pacified,

4. Zhōu Shì (周巿) returned from Dí (狄).
Arriving in the territory of Wèi (魏),
he wished to establish the former Wèi (魏)公子 (gōngzǐ) Nínglíng-jūn Jiù (寧陵君咎) as king.

He was unable to obtain Wèi (魏).

"When the world is in chaos,

The lords strongly urged Shì (巿) to become king,
but Shì (巿) ultimately declined.
He welcomed Wèi Jiù (魏咎) from Chén (陳),
after five appeals,
King Chén (陳) then sent him,
establishing Jiù (咎) as King of Wèi (魏),
and Shì (巿) as Chancellor of Wèi (魏).
5. That year,
Èrshì (二世) deposed Wèi (衞) Lord Jiǎo (角) as a commoner,
and the Wèi (衞) sacrificial offerings ceased.
Among the states enfeoffed by Zhōu (周),
Wèi (衞) was the last to perish.

Volume Two: The Second Emperor.
1. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Sīzhōu (泗州)監 (jiān) Píng (平) led troops to besiege Pèigōng (沛公) at Fēng (豐).
Sīchuān (泗川) Commandery is Sīshuǐ (泗水) Commandery.

Qī (戚),

Both armies dispersed,
fleeing to Chén (陳),
and King Chén (陳) executed Dèng Yuè (鄧說).
3 Èrshì (二世) repeatedly reprimanded Lǐ Sī (李斯):
"Holding the position of a Sāngōng (三公),
how can you allow bandits to be like this!"
Lǐ Sī (李斯) was afraid,
valuing his noble rank and emoluments,
not knowing what to do,
so he accommodated Èrshì's (二世) wishes,
and replied in a memorial:
"A wise lord,
must be one who can implement the art of 'supervision and enforcement.'
Suǒyǐn (索隱) says: 'Dū (督)'
means to inspect;
to investigate their crimes,
and hold them accountable with punishments.
It is called
'taking all-under-heaven as shackles'
for no other reason
than this:
if one cannot supervise and enforce,
but instead labors his own body for the people of all-under-heaven,
like Yáo (堯) and Yǔ (禹),
then it is called 'shackles.'
Zhìgù (桎梏)
are restraints;
those on the feet are called zhì (桎),
and those on the hands are called gù (梏).
Zhì (桎),
pronounced zhí rì fān.
Gù (梏),
pronounced gū wò fān.
To practice the way of supervision and enforcement
is to wholly indulge oneself with all-under-heaven;
but merely to labor one's body and weary one's spirit,
sacrificing oneself for the common people,
is to be a servant of the black-haired multitude,
not one who possesses all-under-heaven.
How can this be worthy of esteem!
Therefore, if an enlightened ruler can implement the art of supervision and enforcement and make sole decisions from above,
then power will not reside with the ministers and subordinates.
Only then can he obliterate the path of benevolence and righteousness,
suppress the arguments of remonstrance and persuasion,
act with an unbridled and arbitrary heart
and no one would dare oppose him.
In this way,
all ministers and the common people would not have enough time to rectify their own faults,
how would they dare contemplate rebellion!"
Èrshì (二世) was pleased.
Thereupon, the practice of supervision and enforcement became even stricter.
Those who taxed the people most heavily were considered enlightened officials;
those who killed the most people were considered loyal ministers.
The punished were half the number on the roads,
and the dead accumulated daily in the markets.
The Qín (秦) people became increasingly terrified and contemplated rebellion.
4 Zhào Lǐ Liáng (趙李良) had already pacified Chángshān (常山).
Last year,
the King of Zhào (趙王) sent Lǐ Liáng (李良) to conquer Chángshān (常山).
The King of Zhào (趙王) again sent Liáng (良) to conquer Tàiyuán (太原);
upon reaching Yòuyì (右邑),
Qín (秦) forces blocked Jǐngxíng (井陘),
and he could not advance.
Bān Zhì (班志) says,
Shíyì (石邑) county belonged to Chángshān Jùn (常山郡),
and Jǐngxíng Shān (井陘山) was to its west.
Sāi (塞),
pronounced xì zé fān.
Xíng (陘),
pronounced xíng.
Liáng (良) received the letter but did not trust it,
so he returned to Hándān (邯鄲)
to request more troops.
Before he arrived,
he encountered the King of Zhào's (趙王) sister coming out to drink.
Liáng (良) saw her from a distance,
took her for the King,
and prostrated himself by the roadside.
The King's sister was drunk,
did not recognize him as a general,
and had a rider offer an apology to Lǐ Liáng (李良).
Lǐ Liáng (李良) had always been esteemed.
He rose,
ashamed before his retinue.
He bowed and rose,
looking back at his retinue with shame.
Cóng (從),
pronounced cái yòng fān.
"All-under-heaven is rebelling against Qín (秦),
and the capable are established first.
Moreover, the King of Zhào (趙王) has always been inferior to the General.
Now, his daughter does not even alight from her carriage for the General,
please pursue and kill her!"
Lǐ Liáng (李良) had already received the Qín (秦) letter and
firmly intended to defect from Zhào (趙),
but had not yet decided.
Incensed by this,
he sent men to pursue and kill the King's sister,
and then led his troops to attack Hándān (邯鄲).
Hándān (邯鄲) was unaware,
and he ended up killing the King of Zhào (趙王) and Shào Sāo (邵騷).
Many people in Zhào (趙) were spies for Zhāng Ěr (張耳) and Chén Yú (陳餘),
which is why these two alone managed to escape.
'Yǐ gù zhě' (以故者)
means 'because of this reason.'
5 Qín Jiā (秦嘉) from Chén (陳) and Zhū Jīshí (朱雞石) from Fúlǐ (符離) and others raised an army,
besieging the Administrator of Dōnghǎi (東海) at Tán (郯).
"Chén (陳)"
should be
"Líng (凌)";
Chén Shèng Zhuàn (陳勝傳) writes
"Qín Jiā (秦嘉) from Líng (凌)."
Qín (秦)
is a surname;
during the Qīnqiū (秦秋) period,
Lǔ (魯) had Qín Jǐnfù (秦堇父).
Bān Zhì (班志) says: Dōnghǎi Jùn (東海郡)
was established by Hàn Gāodì (漢高帝);
Yīng Shào (應劭) notes: it is the Qín (秦) Tán Jùn (郯郡).
I (Yú, 餘) note that what Péi Yīn (裴駰) refers to as the thirty-six commanderies
originally did not include Tán Jùn (郯郡);
the Hàn (漢) Dōnghǎi Jùn (東海郡) merely governed Tán (郯).
He sent Wǔpíng Jūn Pàn (武平君畔) to be a general,
overseeing the army at Tán (郯).
Qín Jiā (秦嘉) did not accept the appointment,
and established himself as Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬);
disliking being subordinate to Wǔpíng Jūn (武平君),
he told his military officers:
"Wǔpíng Jūn (武平君) is young,
and knows nothing of military affairs,
do not listen to him!"
He then falsely issued a royal command to kill Wǔpíng Jūn Pàn (武平君畔).
6 Èrshì (二世) further dispatched Chángshǐ (長史) Sīmǎ Xīn (司馬欣) and Dǒng Yì (董翳) to assist Zhāng Hán (章邯) in attacking the bandits.
At that time, Zhāng Hán (章邯) was the supreme general,
leading troops to the east for campaigns,
so Xīn (欣) was made Chángshǐ (長史) to assist him.
According to Xiàng Jí Zhuàn (項籍傳),
Yì (翳) was a Dūwèi (都尉).
Xìng Pǔ (姓譜) says: Liáoshú'ān's (飂叔安) descendant Dǒng Fù (董父) loved dragons,
Emperor Shùn (帝舜) praised him,
and thus bestowed upon him the surname Dǒng (董).
They attacked Chén (陳) pillar state Fáng Jūn (房君)
and killed him;
they then advanced to attack Zhāng Hè's (張賀) army west of Chén (陳).
The King of Chén (陳王) oversaw the battle.
Zhāng Hè (張賀) died.
In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) said: "The twelfth month of Qín (秦)
is the ninth month of Xià (夏)."
Chén Zàn (臣瓚) said: "It is the month when chǒu (丑) is established."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Shǐjì (史記) states: "In the tenth month of Húhài's (胡亥) second year,
Gé Yīng (葛嬰) was executed;
in the eleventh month,
Zhōu Wén (周文) died;
in the twelfth month,
Chén Shè (陳涉) died." Zàn's (瓚) statement is correct.
Chén Wáng (陳王) went to Rǔyīn (汝陰).
Zhī (之),
means "to go."
Arriving at Xiàchéngfù (下城父),
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Xiàchéngfù (下城父)
is a place name,
located east of Chéngfù (城父) county in Pèijùn (沛郡)."
Liú Zhāo (劉昭) said: "Shānsāng (山桑) county in Rǔnán (汝南),
formerly belonged to Pèi (沛),
and had the settlement of Xiàchéngfù (下城父)."
Fù (父),
is pronounced fǔ (甫).
Initially,
after Chén Shè (陳涉) became king,
all his old friends went to seek refuge with him.
His wife's father also went,
but Chén Wáng (陳王) treated him as one of the many guests,
bowing with a long salute but not prostrating.
His wife's father angrily said:
"Relying on chaos to usurp a title,
and disrespecting elders,
you will not last long!"
He left without a word.
Chén Wáng (陳王) knelt and apologized,
but thereafter paid him no more attention.
The guests coming and going became even more relaxed and informal,
speaking of Chén Wáng's (陳王) past affairs.
Someone advised Chén Wáng (陳王), saying:
"These guests are foolish and ignorant,
wantonly speaking nonsense,
and slighting your authority."
Chén Wáng (陳王) executed him.
All his old friends then withdrew themselves,
and from this point, no one close to Chén Wáng (陳王) remained.
Chén Wáng (陳王) appointed Zhū Fáng (朱防) as Zhōngzhèng (中正),
and Hú Wǔ (胡武) as Sīguò (司過),
to supervise and control the officials.
When the generals who had captured territory arrived,
if their orders were not correct,
they were immediately arrested and punished.
He regarded strict scrutiny as loyalty;
for those whose conduct he disapproved of,
he did not hand them over to the magistrates,
but dealt with them himself.
Because of this, the generals did not attach themselves to him,
which is why he was defeated.
The historian states that Chén Wáng (陳王) abandoned his relatives and old friends,
and subsequently died at the hands of Zhuāng Jiǎ (莊賈).
Therefore, the text first uses the words "old friends" to begin the narrative,
then discusses the matter of slighting his wife's father,
and next the matter of the guests.
The guest had previously worked as a hired farmer with Chén Wáng (陳王);
when Chén Wáng (陳王) occupied Chén (陳) and became king,
the guest blocked his path to seek an audience.
Chén Wáng (陳王) took him in his carriage and returned home with him;
later, because the guest spoke of his past affairs,
he killed him.
"Slighting his authority" (輕威者),
means to diminish the gravitas of his authority as ruler.
Zhuān (顓),
is the same as zhuān (專).
Chén Wáng's (陳王) former attendant and general Lǚ Chén (呂臣) formed the Cāngtóu (蒼頭) army.
Wèi (魏) had two hundred thousand Cāngtóu (蒼頭) soldiers,
indicating that there were Cāngtóu (蒼tóu) armies even before this time.
Yīng Shào (應劭) said: "At that time, all soldiers wore green headscarves,
hence they were called Cāngtóu (蒼頭)."
Fú Qián (服虔) said: "Cāngtóu (蒼頭)
refers to soldiers with green cloth headscarves,
like the Chìméi (赤眉) designation to distinguish themselves."
Bān Zhì (班志) states: "Xīnyáng (新陽) county belonged to Rǔnán (汝南) commandery";
Yīng Shào (應劭) said: "It is on the south side of Xīnshuǐ (新水)."
Kuòdìzhì (括地志) states: "The old city of Xīnyáng (新陽)
is forty-two lǐ southwest of Zhēnyáng (真陽) county in Yùzhōu (豫州)."
Lǚ Chén (呂臣) took
it, killed Zhuāng Jiǎ (莊賈),
and again established Chén (陳) as Chǔ (楚);
he buried Chén Wáng (陳王) in Dàng (碭),
giving him the posthumous title of Yǐnwáng (隱王).
Originally,
Chén Wáng (陳王) ordered Sòng Liú (宋留) of Zhì (銍) to lead troops to pacify Nányáng (南陽)
and enter Wǔguān (武關).
After Liú (留) had conquered Nányáng (南陽),
he heard that Chén Wáng (陳王) had died,
and Nányáng (南陽) had reverted to Qín (秦);
Sòng Liú (宋留) surrendered with his army.
Èrshì (二世) dismembered Liú (留) by chariots as a public display.
7 Wèi (魏) general Zhōu Shì (周巿) led troops to capture
Fēng (豐) and Pèi (沛),
and sent someone to recruit Yōng Chǐ (雍齒).
Yōng Chǐ (雍齒) had always been unwilling to serve Pèigōng (沛公),
and so surrendered Fēng (豐) to Wèi (魏).
Yǎ (雅),
means "always" or "originally."
He was unsuccessful.
8 Zhào (趙) Zhāng Ěr (張耳) and Chén Yú (陳餘) gathered their scattered troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men,
and attacked Lǐ Liáng (李良);
Liáng (良) was defeated
and fled back to Zhāng Hán (章邯).
A guest advised Ěr (耳) and Yú (餘), saying:
"You two lords are sojourners,
and if you wish to attach yourselves to Zhào (趙), it will be difficult to stand independently;
if you enthrone a descendant of Zhào (趙)
and assist him with righteousness,
you can achieve success."
So they sought and found Zhào Xiē (趙歇).
In spring,
the first month,
Ěr (耳) and Yú (餘) enthroned Xiē (歇) as King of Zhào (趙),
residing in Xìndū (信都).
Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) renamed Xìndū (信都) as Xiāngguó (襄國);
Hàn (漢) later restored it to Xìndū (信都) county,
belonging to Xìndū (信都) kingdom;
Later Hàn (後漢) again called it Xiāngguó (襄國).
9 Dōngyáng Níng Jūn (東陽甯君) and Qín Jiā (秦嘉)
Wén Yǐng (文穎) said: "Qín Jiā (秦嘉)
was a man from Dōngyáng (東陽) commandery,
serving as Lord of Níng (甯) county."
Chén Zàn (臣瓚) said: "Chén Shèng (陳勝) Biography:
'Língrén (凌人) Qín Jiā (秦嘉)';
if so, Jiā (嘉) was not from Dōngyáng (東陽).
Jiā (嘉) rose in Tán (郯),
was titled Dàsīmǎ (大司馬),
and was also not Lord of Níng (甯) county.
Dōngyáng Níng Jūn (東陽甯君) is one person,
and Qín Jiā (秦嘉) is another person."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Zàn's (瓚) statement is correct."
Dōngyáng (東陽)
refers to the county of allegiance;
Níng Jūn (甯君)
refers to someone with the surname Níng (甯),
who was at that time called Jūn (君).
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: "Descendants of the Wèi (衛) minister Níng (甯) clan;
also in Jìn (晉) there was Níng Yíng (甯嬴),
who took his fief as his surname."
They then enthroned Jǐng Jū (景駒) as King of Chǔ (楚),
led troops to Fāngyǔ (方與),
intending to attack the Qín (秦) army below Dìngtáo (定陶);
Bān Zhì (班志) states: "Fāngyǔ (方與) county belonged to Shānyáng (山陽) commandery,
Dìngtáo (定陶) county belonged to Jìyīn (濟陰) commandery."
Shǐjì Zhèngyì (史記正義) says: "Fāngyǔ (方與)
is now Jìzhōu (濟州) county;
Dìngtáo (定陶) is now Cáozhōu (曹州) county."
Fāngyǔ (方與),
is pronounced fángyù (房預).
They wished to combine forces and advance together.
The King of Qí (齊) said:
"Chén Wáng (陳王) was defeated,
and his fate is unknown.
How can Chǔ (楚) enthrone a king without consulting Qí (齊)?"
Gōngsūn Qìng (公孫慶) said:
"If Qí (齊) can enthrone a king without consulting Chǔ (楚),
why should Chǔ (楚) consult Qí (齊) to enthrone a king?
Moreover, Chǔ (楚) initiated the undertaking,
and should issue orders to all under heaven."
"Initiated the undertaking" (首事),
means to be the first to raise troops to attack Qín (秦).
The Qín (秦) Left and Right Commanders
again attacked Chén (陳),
and took it.
Suǒyǐn (索隱) said: "Zuǒ (左) and Yòu Jiào (右校)
are the Left and Right Commanders."
Jiào (校),
is pronounced hùjiāo (戶教) fān (翻).
The scattered troops gathered again.
Rú Chún (如淳) said: "Jiào (徼),
means to gather;
to gather the scattered soldiers again."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Jiào (徼),
is pronounced gōngyáo (工堯) fān (翻)."
I (Shīgǔ) think that according to Rú (如) clan's explanation,
it should be pronounced yúyáo (於堯) fān (翻).
Pō (番),
refers to Pōyáng (番陽) county,
which belonged to Yùzhāng (豫章) commandery in Hàn (漢).
Yīng Bù (英布) was a bandit in the middle of the Jiāng (江) River;
the magistrate of Pōyáng (番陽), Wú Ruì (吳芮), gave his daughter to him in marriage,
hence he was called the Pō (番) bandit.
Pō (番),
is pronounced púhé (蒲何) fān (翻).
They defeated the Qín (秦) army at Qīngbō (青波),
and again established Chén (陳) as Chǔ (楚).
Yīng Bù (黥布) was
from Liù (六).
Liù (六)
was one of the Liù Guó (六國) of the Spring and Autumn period.
Under Qín (秦), it was a xiàn (縣)
belonging to Jiǔjiāng Jùn (九江郡).
Under Hàn (漢), it belonged to Liù'ān Guó (六安國).
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) says: The old city of Liù (六)
is one hundred thirty lǐ (里) south of Ānfēng Xiàn (安豐縣) in Shòuzhōu (壽州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Today's Guǎngjì Xiàn (廣濟縣) in Qízhōu (蘄州) is the Liù Xiàn (六縣) of Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢).
Yīng Bù (英布) made Liù (六) his capital,
and its ancient city still remains.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) says: The Yīng (英) surname originated from the Yǎn (偃) clan.
Gāo Táo (皋陶)'s descendants were enfeoffed in Yīng (英),
and took this as their surname.
As a convict, he was sentenced to labor on Lì Shān (驪山).
There were several hundred thousand laborers on Lì Shān (驪山).
Bù (布) associated with all the leaders and strongmen among them,
and then led his companions.
Cáo (曹)
means "group" or "class."
Wú Ruì (吳芮), the magistrate of Pányáng (番陽),
was very popular among the common people in the Jiānghú (江湖) region,
and was called the Pán Jūn (番君).
Bù (布) went to see him,
and his followers already numbered several thousand.
Pán Jūn (番君) then married his daughter to him
and had him lead his troops to attack Qín (秦).
10 Chǔ (楚) King Jǐng Jū (景駒) was in Liú (留).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says
Liú Xiàn (留縣) belonged to Chǔ Guó (楚國).
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) says: Liú Chéng (留城) is fifty lǐ (里) southeast of Pèi Xiàn (沛縣) in Xúzhōu (徐州),
which is where Zhāng Liáng (張良) was enfeoffed.
Zhāng Liáng (張良) also gathered over a hundred youths and wanted to follow Jǐng Jū (景駒),
but on the way encountered Pèi Gōng (沛公),
and so joined him.
Pèi Gōng (沛公) appointed Liáng (良) as a Jiáng (⿸广既將).
A Jiáng (⿸广既將) probably commanded cavalry.
Pèi Gōng (沛公) admired him
and often used his strategies.
When Liáng (良) spoke to others,
they did not understand.
Liáng (良) said,
"Pèi Gōng (沛公) must be Heaven-bestowed!"
Therefore, he stayed and did not leave.
Zhāng Liáng (張良) began following Pèi Gōng (沛公) from this point.
Pèi Gōng (沛公) and Liáng (良) both went to see Jǐng Jū (景駒),
wanting to request troops to attack Fēng (豐).
At this time, Zhāng Hán (章邯)'s Sīmǎ (司馬) was leading troops north to pacify the Chǔ (楚) region.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: (夷)
is the ancient character for "yí" (夷).
The Lèipiān (類篇) says: It is the ancient character for "rén" (仁);
also pronounced yán-zhī (延知).
They reached Dàng (碭).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says
Xiàng Xiàn (相縣) was the administrative seat of Pèi Jùn (沛郡).
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) says: The old city of Xiàng (相)
is ninety lǐ (里) west of Fúlí Xiàn (符離縣) in Xúzhōu (徐州).
Xiàng (相)
is pronounced xī-liàng (息亮).
Dàng (碭)
is pronounced tú-láng (徒郎).
They fought west of Xiāo (蕭).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says
Xiāo Xiàn (蕭縣) belonged to Pèi Jùn (沛郡);
in the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Xúzhōu (徐州).
Xiāo Xī (蕭西)
means west of Xiāo Xiàn (蕭縣).
They returned
and regrouped their forces in Liú (留).
In the second month,
they attacked Dàng (碭).
After three days,
they captured it.
They took six thousand Dàng (碭) soldiers,
making a total of nine thousand with their previous forces.
In the third month,
they attacked Xiàyì (下邑)
and captured it.
The Bān Zhì (班志) says
Xiàyì Xiàn (下邑縣) belonged to Liáng Guó (梁國).
It was not captured.
11 Shào Píng (召平) of Guǎnglíng (廣陵) was soliciting Guǎnglíng (廣陵) for King Chén (陳王),
but had not yet taken it.
Guǎnglíng Xiàn (廣陵縣) belonged to Jiǔjiāng Jùn (九江郡).
The Bān Zhì (班志) lists it as the capital of Guǎnglíng Guó (廣陵國);
in the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Yángzhōu (揚州).
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) says: The Shào (召) surname
descended from Shào Gōng Shì (召公奭), King Wén (文王) of Zhōu (周)'s son.
Shào (召)
is pronounced shí-zhào (寔照).
As Zhāng Hán (章邯) was about to arrive,
he crossed the river
and, falsely using King Chén (陳王)'s order,
appointed Xiàng Liáng (項梁) as the Supreme Pillar of the State of Chǔ (楚上柱國),
saying:
"The east of the Jiāng (江) has been pacified.
Quickly lead your troops west to attack Qín (秦)!"
Liáng (梁) then crossed the river westward with eight thousand men.
He heard that Chén Yīng (陳嬰) had already subdued Dōngyáng (東陽).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says
Dōngyáng Xiàn (東陽縣) belonged to Línhuái Jùn (臨淮郡);
Emperor Míng (明帝) reallocated it to Xiàpī (下邳);
