13 The Chamberlain of the Palace, Zhào Gāo,
(Biāo says: The Chamberlain of the Palace [Lángzhōnglìng]
was a Qin official [Qín guān]
in charge of the palace gates and side entrances.
Minister Zàn says: He was in charge of all the officials within the palace,
hence the name Lángzhōnglìng;
Emperor Wǔ changed it to Guānglùxūn.
He executed many people out of personal vendetta.
Fearing that high officials would report this to the court,
he said to Èrshì:
"The reason why the Son of Heaven is revered
is simply that his voice is heard,
but none of his ministers may see his face.
Moreover, Your Majesty is in the bloom of youth,"
meaning 'young,'
this refers to being very young.
"If you now sit in court
and your rebukes or appointments are inappropriate,
you will appear deficient to your high officials,
which is not how to demonstrate divine wisdom to the world.
It would be better for Your Majesty to stay deeply secluded in the forbidden palace."
Cài Yì says: Originally, the forbidden palace [jìnzhōng]
refers to gates and chambers that were restricted;
officials who were not attendants were not allowed to enter without permission.
Moving along the leopard-tail path was also considered within the forbidden palace.
"When matters arise, you will have a way to gauge them.
If you do this,
then high officials will not dare to present doubtful matters,
and the world will call you a sagely ruler."
Èrshì adopted his plan,
and thereafter did not sit in court to see his high officials,
but always remained in the forbidden palace.
Zhào Gāo, as a palace attendant, handled all affairs.

(Biāo says: According to the Qin system, Palace Attendants [shìzhōng], Left and Right Cao [zuǒyòucáo], various clerks [zhūlì], Cavalier Attendants [sǎnqí], and Regular Palace Attendants [zhōngchángshì] were all additional offices.
Those appointed might be marquises, ministers, grandees, generals, commanders, commandants, imperial secretaries, imperial physicians, or grand cook chiefs,
even up to Chamberlain of the Palace, with no fixed number,
often as many as several tens of people.
Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants were allowed to enter the forbidden palace.
Yìng Shào says: They served the Son of Heaven,
hence the name shìzhōng.
The Hòuhàn Zhì says: Shìzhōng,
ranked at two thousand dàn,
were in charge of attending on the left and right,
guiding various affairs,
and responding to imperial questions.)
Gāo heard that Lǐ Sī had been speaking against him,
so he went to see the Chancellor and said:
"There are many bandits east of the pass.
The emperor is now urgently increasing conscripted labor
to build the Epáng Palace and
gather useless things like dogs and horses.
I wish to admonish him,
but my position is low.
This is truly a matter for Your Lordship;
why do you not admonish him?"
Lǐ Sī replied:
"Indeed,
I have long wished to speak about this.
But currently, the emperor does not sit in court
and always stays in the deep palace.
What I wish to say
cannot be transmitted;
if I wish to see him,
there is no opportune moment."
Zhào Gāo said:
"If Your Lordship can truly admonish him,
I will arrange an opportune moment for you
and inform you."
Thereupon, Zhào Gāo, while
Èrshì was engaged in feasting and revelry,
with women in attendance,
sent someone to inform the Chancellor:
"His Majesty is now at leisure,
you may present your affairs."
The Chancellor arrived at the palace gate and requested an audience.
This happened three times.
Èrshì was enraged and said:
"I always have many days of leisure,
but the Chancellor does not come;
when I am enjoying private revelry,
the Chancellor always comes to request an audience!
Does the Chancellor look down on me,
or does he think I am stubborn?"
To look down on me [shǎo wǒ]
means to treat me lightly as being young.
To think I am stubborn [gù wǒ]
means to treat me lightly as being crude and ignorant.
"Furthermore, the Sand Dune plot
involved the Chancellor."
(The matter is seen in the previous volume, Shǐhuáng's thirty-seventh year.)
Yǔ [與]
is read as yù [預].
"Yet the Chancellor's status has not increased.
His intention must also be to partition land and become a king.
Moreover, if Your Majesty does not ask me,
I dare not speak.
The Chancellor's eldest son, Lǐ Yóu, is the Administrator of Sānchuān.
The Chu bandits Chén Shèng and others are all from counties near the Chancellor's residence."
Bàngxiàn [傍縣]
means nearby counties.
Lǐ Sī
was from Shàngcài in Rǔnán;
Chén Shèng
was from Yángchéng in Yǐngchuān: Rǔnán and Yǐngchuān are close.
"When they passed through Sānchuān city,
the administrator
refused to attack.
Gāo heard that their documents were in correspondence,
but has not yet obtained full verification,
so he has not dared to report it.
Moreover, the Chancellor resides outside [the court]
and wields more power than Your Majesty."
Èrshì believed this to be true
and wanted to investigate the Chancellor.
Fearing it was not verified,
he first sent someone to investigate the circumstances of the Administrator of Sānchuān's communication with the bandits.
When Lǐ Sī heard this,
he then submitted a memorial criticizing Zhào Gāo, saying:
"Gāo is adept at both bringing benefit and causing harm,
no different from Your Majesty.
In the past, Tián Cháng served as Chancellor to Qí Jiǎngōng,
usurping his favors and prestige,
gaining the support of the common people below,
and gaining the support of the various ministers above.
In the end, he assassinated Jiǎngōng and seized the state of Qí."
(The matter is seen in Zuǒ Zhuàn.)
Zú [卒]
is read as zìxù fān.
"Now Gāo harbors wicked and unrestrained ambitions,
and performs dangerous and rebellious acts.
The wealth of his private household
is like that of the Tián family in Qí.
Moreover, he is insatiably greedy,
relentlessly seeking profit,
and his influence rivals that of the ruler."
(It means that Zhào Gāo, holding power in the court,
had a position of influence second only to the ruler.)
"He abuses Your Majesty's authority and trust.
His ambition is like that of Hán Yí who was Chancellor to Hán Ān."
(Suǒyǐn says:
"Yí" [⿰王巳]
is also written as
both pronounced Yí.
He was a Hán grandee [Hán dàfū]
who assassinated his ruler, Dàogōng.
However, there was no Dàogōng in Hán,
perhaps the successor ruler of Zhèng.
Upon examination of the table, Hán Yí served Zhāohóu.
Four generations passed from Zhāohóu down to King Ān, so Lǐ Sī's statement is incorrect.
I observe Lǐ Sī's intent in writing this memorial:
It is precisely because Húhài's doom and the downfall of the state were imminent
that he pointed to Hán Ān, using the event of his employing Hán Yí and the downfall of Hán to alarm him.
At the time of Hán Ān,
there must have been a minister like Hán Yí,
it is simply that history omitted his deeds.

Èrshì genuinely loved Zhào
Gāo

At this time,

The Right Chancellor Féng Qùjí, Left Chancellor Lǐ Sī, and General Féng Jié, advanced and remonstrated, saying:

‘Shù’ [garrison],

‘Zhuǎn’ [land transport],

Èr Shì said:

‘Zhǔ zhòng’ [lord holds great power],

He ordered Féng Qùjí, Lǐ Sī, and Féng Jié to be handed over to the officials,

16 Later, in the ninth month,
Wén Yǐng says: This is the intercalary ninth month.
At that time, the calendar system was defunct,
and the intercalary month was not known,
hence it was called "later ninth month".
Rú Chún says: At that time, Qín took the tenth month as the beginning of the year,
so the ninth month was the end of the year;
the "later ninth month" was the intercalary month.
Shī Gǔ says: Wén's explanation is incorrect.
If the calendar system was defunct and the intercalary month unknown,
then it should simply be called the tenth month,
there should not be a "later ninth month".
It is likely that Qín’s calendar system
always placed the intercalary month at the end of the year when it was due;
this idea must have been taken from the Zuǒ Zhuàn's "return the surplus to the end."
How can this be proven?
According to the Hàn Biǎo and Shǐ Jì,
before the Hàn dynasty changed the Qín calendar,
up to Empress Gāo and Emperor Wén,
"later ninth month" was frequently recorded;
from this we know it was definitely so,
not due to a defunct calendar.
Gòngfù says: I say that Yán's explanation of "later ninth month" is also not exhaustive.
If Qín knew to place intercalary months in the calendar,
why were they all designated as the ninth month?
It is probable that Sīmǎ Shì, when compiling the Shǐ Jì,
having already referred to Qín's first month as the tenth month,
consequently generalized all intercalary months as "later ninth month."
Thus, Sīmǎ Shì narrated it this way,
it was not a Qín law.
